prompt: A dependency starts failing with intermittent resets. A team adds an immediate retry on every failed call, with no limit. Load rises. What is the likely result?

options.text: A retry storm — one of the mechanisms by which a local problem becomes a cascading failure
Improved transient success, since resets are exactly what retries are for
options.feedback: Retries improve transient success only with backoff, jitter, budgets, and idempotency. An immediate, unlimited retry has none of the four.

options.text: No change, because the dependency was already the bottleneck
options.feedback: The dependency was already struggling, and now each failed call becomes several. Retry storms, unbounded queues, synchronized autoscaling, shared connection-pool exhaustion, and slow dependencies create cascading failure.

options.text: Load shedding will engage and reject the excess
options.feedback: Load shedding rejects excess work before all requests time out, and nothing here added it. A mechanism you have not built does not bound the traffic you have just created.

explanation: Retries improve transient success only with backoff, jitter, budgets, and idempotency. The shop page's version is a bounded retry budget covering rare resets — the same instinct with a limit on it. Without those, retry storms, unbounded queues, synchronized autoscaling, shared connection-pool exhaustion, and slow dependencies create cascading failure.

back: Scaling preserves acceptable service as demand grows; resilience preserves useful behavior when components slow down or fail.
Vertical scaling is operationally simple but finite; horizontal scaling adds coordination and data-distribution challenges.
It makes load balancing and failover inconsistent. Stateless request handling instead lets any healthy instance serve a request.
It increases availability but can multiply cost and correlated misconfiguration.

front: A health check that tests only the process
back: It admits instances that cannot serve.

prompt: A reviewer reads an `orders` table. It has `is_paid` and `is_shipped` boolean flags, a `total` stored as floating point, and the customer's display name copied onto every row with nothing marking that copy as historical. No column in the table is nullable. Which problems named in this lesson are present?

options.text: The boolean flags hide a multi-step lifecycle
Money stored as floating point loses exact decimal intent
The copied display name will create silent disagreement
Nullable columns are mixing several meanings
The copied display name is fine, because it is an explicitly historical copy

explanation: Boolean fields hide multi-step lifecycles, money stored as floating point loses exact decimal intent, and copying display names into many records creates silent disagreement — unless the copy is explicitly historical, and this one is not. That qualifier is the whole difference between this row and the order's commercial snapshot. Nullable columns do mix several meanings, but the stem rules them out here.

prompt: An order records the delivery address used for that order, but references the customer identity rather than copying anything about the customer. Why do the two facts get opposite treatment?

options.text: The address that mattered is the one used then, while a customer is an entity that maintains identity through change
Addresses change more often than customers do
options.feedback: Nothing in this lesson ranks how often either changes. The distinction is what each field is for: one holds the state of an entity now, the other holds what was true at the time of the order.

options.text: Normalization requires the address to be duplicated and the customer to be referenced
options.feedback: Normalization avoids storing the same fact in multiple places, so it argues against the copy rather than for it. The copy is a deliberate denormalization, and what makes it safe is that it is explicitly historical.

options.text: Copying the customer identity would violate the constraints that reject impossible states
options.feedback: Database constraints reject impossible states, but nothing here makes a copied customer identity impossible. The reason is about which fact each field is meant to hold.

explanation: Entities maintain identity through change, so referencing the customer gets whoever that customer is now. The delivery address used for that order is a fact about the order, and recording it is a copy that is explicitly historical rather than a copy that will silently disagree. One reference and one copy in the same record, for opposite reasons.

prompt: A team is choosing how to represent an order. Match each representation to what this lesson says it favors or costs.

pairs.right: frequently used data kept together, shared facts duplicated
how state changed, at the cost of projections and versioned interpretation
real-world uniqueness, in a value that may change

distractors: stable internally
identity maintained through change
explanation: Normalized relational models favor integrity and flexible joins. Document aggregates keep frequently used data together but duplicate shared facts. Event histories preserve how state changed but require projections and versioned interpretation. Natural keys can enforce real-world uniqueness but may change. The two distractors come from elsewhere in the lesson: surrogate identifiers are stable internally, and identity maintained through change is what makes something an entity rather than a value object.

back: Identifies facts, identities, relationships, constraints, and lifecycles, then represents them so required operations remain correct and understandable.

front: The questions a model starts from
back: What fact must survive? What identifies it? Which rules are always true? Who owns changes? Which queries and histories matter? What can be recomputed?
An entity maintains identity through change; a value object is defined by its contents.
Normalization avoids storing the same fact in multiple places; deliberate denormalization stores a derived copy to improve a known access path.
They distinguish occurrence, recording, and update time.

prompt: A marketplace stores each order as one self-contained document. A rule that has to hold across many orders at once keeps being violated, even though every individual document is valid. Which of this lesson's pressures is that?

options.text: Cross-document invariants, the common pressure on the document model
Horizontal partitioning
options.feedback: That is the pressure on the relational model, which is strong at constraints, joins and transactions and is pressed when it has to distribute itself.

options.text: Secondary query needs
options.feedback: That is the key-value pressure. It appears when direct lookup is not the only access you need, not when a rule spans several records.

options.text: General transactional workloads
options.feedback: That is the graph pressure. Graph models are strong at relationship traversal and pressed by general transactional work.

explanation: Document stores are strong at aggregate retrieval and flexible shape, and their common pressure is cross-document invariants. Every document being valid on its own is the shape of the problem rather than evidence against it. It is also the opening scene's real fault: the store was chosen for peak scale before ordinary correctness was modeled, and the pressure arrived before the scale did.

prompt: A team runs one relational database. They are about to add a search index for discovery and a cache for popular product summaries. Which of these does this lesson say they are taking on?

options.text: More expertise to maintain
More backup work
More security work
More reconciliation work
The search index becomes an additional authority for product facts
Writing to both new stores directly is safe as long as both writes return success

explanation: Polyglot persistence fits tools to jobs but multiplies expertise, backup, security, and reconciliation work — four multipliers, all of them ongoing. Neither distractor holds. Specialized stores may support caching, search, analytics, graphs, or high-volume event access without becoming the authority for every fact, and dual writes to independent stores drift without a durable coordination pattern, which is why the marketplace in this lesson publishes committed changes through an outbox instead.

prompt: A team is deciding where to perform a join. Complete what each choice adds.
template: Join in the database and it centralizes optimization and {{1}}. Join in application code and it adds round trips and partial {{2}}.
explanation: Joining in a database centralizes optimization and consistency; joining in application code adds round trips and partial failure. The two costs are not the same kind of thing — round trips are latency, partial failure is an outcome — which is why this lesson treats where to join as a design decision rather than a preference.

back: Document, key-value, wide-column, and graph models, which optimize different access and distribution patterns. It is a grouping rather than a single alternative to relational.

front: What a database choice should follow
back: Invariants, query shapes, scale, latency, availability, and operational capability — rather than a generic category label.

The primary database often holds authoritative application state, while specialized stores may support caching, search, analytics, graphs, or high-volume event access without becoming the authority for every fact.
It moves responsibility from the database to application readers and migrations. It does not remove schema — the data still has a shape, and what moves is who has to know it.
They drift without a durable coordination pattern. The marketplace in this lesson avoids that by publishing committed changes through an outbox.

prompt: A counter is updated by reading it, adding one, and writing it back. Under concurrent load the stored total ends up lower than the number of updates that succeeded. Every write returned success, and nothing was rolled back. What happened?

options.text: Read-modify-write without concurrency control lost updates
A response was lost after commit, so the client outcome is unknown
options.feedback: That failure leaves a client unsure what happened while the record is correct. Here the record itself is wrong, and every client was told the truth.

options.text: Retrying a transaction that calls a remote service duplicated effects
options.feedback: Duplicated effects would push the total above the number of requests, not below it. Nothing here retries, and nothing here calls a remote service.

options.text: The transactions were held open too long, retaining resources and increasing contention
options.feedback: Long transactions retain resources and increase contention, which surfaces as waiting and conflict rather than as a total that is quietly short.

explanation: Read-modify-write without concurrency control loses updates: two requests read the same value, both add one, and the second write replaces the first. Every write succeeding is the point — nothing failed, which is why the symptom rules out the write path rather than implicating it. The mechanisms that address it put the check and the change in one operation, such as comparing a version before update.

prompt: Match each failure to the mechanism this lesson pairs with it.

pairs.left: Two concurrent edits, and one of them disappears
pairs.right: compare a version before the update

pairs.left: A retry repeats an effect on a remote service
pairs.right: associate repeated commands with one logical effect

pairs.left: A committed change still has to produce a message
pairs.right: record it in the same transaction and deliver it afterward

distractors: define compensating business operations for intermediate states
coordinate participants across stores, at an availability cost
keep the transaction open until the whole workflow finishes
explanation: Optimistic concurrency compares a version before update, closing the gap read-modify-write leaves open. Idempotency associates repeated commands with one logical effect, so a repeated remote call has one outcome. Outbox records connect a committed database change to later message delivery. The distractors are aimed elsewhere: sagas accept intermediate states and define compensating actions, distributed transactions coordinate participants but add availability and operational costs, and long transactions retain resources and increase contention rather than fixing anything.

prompt: A design document says a read path is “eventually consistent” and stops there. According to this lesson, which of these would have to be added before that counts as a design?

options.text: A convergence rule
A time bound
A user state that accounts for the lag
A stronger isolation level on the writing transaction
A distributed transaction spanning both sides

explanation: “Eventually consistent” without a convergence rule, time bound, or user state is not a design: the phrase names an outcome and commits to nothing. Stronger isolation simplifies reasoning about concurrent work but may abort or serialize more of it, and distributed transactions coordinate participants at an availability and operational cost. Neither supplies the missing statement about when the lag ends or what someone sees while it lasts.

back: A grouping of operations into a correctness boundary. Consistency is the separate question of which states and observations a system permits, especially under concurrency, replication, and failure.
Atomicity: do these changes commit together? Isolation: what may concurrent work observe? Durability: what survives acknowledged success? Application consistency adds the actual business rules.
Transactions protect local invariants in a data store. Application workflows coordinate transactions with remote APIs, events, caches, and user-visible status.
Business operations rather than database rollback. Sagas accept intermediate states and define those actions for them.

They permit different anomalies at different costs; PostgreSQL documents Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable behaviors. Stronger isolation simplifies reasoning but may abort or serialize more work.

prompt: The column in the predicate is indexed and the table's statistics were refreshed this morning, yet the planner will not use that index for the query as written. What kind of thing in the query can cause that?
accept: a function or an implicit cast
wrapping the column in a function
hints: The index exists and the statistics are current, so the obstacle is in how the query refers to the column.
One kind is written into the query; the other is supplied silently by a type mismatch.
explanation: Functions or implicit casts can prevent intended index use. Read that against this lesson's mental model — an index is similar to a sorted lookup map from key values to row locations — and a predicate about the result of a function is not a predicate about the keys the index holds. Current statistics rule out the other failure here: stale statistics produce bad estimates rather than preventing use.

prompt: A paged list returns fifty rows a page. It is quick on page one and steadily slower the deeper a reader goes, with the same index used throughout. Which change addresses the cause?

options.text: Page by a bound on the ordering column, so each page asks for rows past a position
Add a covering index so the query stops paying for extra lookups
options.feedback: Covering indexes avoid extra lookups but grow larger, and that cost is the same on page one as on page ninety. It does not explain a slowdown that grows with depth.

options.text: Refresh the table's statistics so the planner stops misestimating
options.feedback: Stale statistics produce bad estimates, which shows up as a poor plan rather than as a good plan doing steadily more work each page.

options.text: Index every column the query touches
options.feedback: Indexing every column wastes resources, and the stem already says an index is in use throughout. What needs changing is what the query asks for.

explanation: Offset pagination scans and discards increasing work, so reaching a deep page costs everything before it even though fifty rows come back each time. The lesson's worked example pages with a `created_at < ?` bound instead — cursor pagination, served by an index beginning with tenant and then creation time, which supports filtering, order, and pagination from one structure.

prompt: A developer reports back on a slow query: they indexed every column appearing in a WHERE clause, timed the query against a development copy, and gave each index a name describing its purpose. Which of these defeat that plan?

options.text: Indexing every column wastes resources
More indexes slow inserts, updates, migrations, and vacuum or compaction
Fast development datasets hide plans that collapse at production cardinality
An index's name asserts nothing; validation needs realistic distributions and an execution plan
More indexes speed inserts and updates along with reads
A covering index would make measuring a plan unnecessary

explanation: The report contains three moves and this lesson refutes each of them. Indexing every column wastes resources, and more indexes speed some reads while slowing inserts, updates, migrations, and vacuum or compaction. Fast development datasets hide plans that collapse at production cardinality, so timing against a development copy establishes nothing about production. And the standing instruction is to validate with realistic tenant distributions and an execution plan rather than relying on the index name. Neither distractor holds: an index consumes storage and must be updated on writes rather than accelerating them, and covering indexes avoid extra lookups without telling you which plan the planner chose.

back: An auxiliary structure that accelerates selected access paths — similar to a sorted lookup map from key values to row locations, saving scanning when the predicate narrows data enough.
It estimates alternative execution strategies and chooses one, based on statistics, available indexes, joins, ordering, and expected cost.
Equality, range, and ordered access for compatible leading keys. Hash, inverted, spatial, and other indexes serve different operators, and composite index order matters.
Covering indexes avoid extra lookups but grow larger; partial indexes target a frequently queried subset.
`EXPLAIN` exposes the chosen plan; the execution-aware variants go further and compare estimates with actual work.

prompt: A team is writing down what each part of their caching setup actually promises. Match each mechanism to what this lesson says it does.

pairs.right: loads on miss and writes to the authority separately
move policy into a cache layer

distractors: improves freshness while extending write latency
protects dependencies while hiding newly created data
explanation: Cache-aside loads on miss and writes to the authority separately. Read-through and write-through move policy into a cache layer. TTLs bound staleness but do not guarantee freshness — bounding describes the worst case, not the current value. Invalidation removes known stale entries. The distractors are tradeoffs from elsewhere in the lesson: synchronous search updates improve freshness while extending write latency, and caching expensive negative results protects dependencies but hides newly created data.

prompt: Product detail responses are cached, and the same catalog feeds a search index. At checkout the system rereads price and inventory from the authority instead of using either. What reason does this lesson give?

options.text: Derived stores may lag, and checkout belongs on the correctness path rather than the acceleration path
The cache key is missing a dimension, so the cached price cannot be trusted
options.feedback: Missing tenant or permission dimensions do leak data, but the detail key here is composed of product, locale and price region. The reason checkout rereads is about which path an answer travels, not about a defective key.

options.text: TTLs bound staleness, so the cached price is only ever slightly out of date
options.feedback: TTLs bound staleness but do not guarantee freshness, and “slightly out of date” is still out of date for a price. That is a reason to reread rather than a reason to trust the projection.

options.text: Search results can reference deleted records
options.feedback: That is a real failure of derived search data, but it is about discovery returning things that are gone — not about why a price is reread at checkout.

explanation: A cache and a search index are both derived data: authority, then change capture, then projection, then query. Derived stores may lag, and interfaces must tolerate or disclose that lag. Checkout is where the system cannot tolerate it, so it takes the direct correctness path and rereads authoritative price and inventory rather than trusting either projection.

prompt: A team moves from synchronous search updates to asynchronous indexing. According to this lesson, which of these follow?

options.text: Writes are isolated from the indexing work
Search results can lag behind committed changes
Something in the interface has to tolerate or disclose that lag
Freshness improves
The search index stops being derived data and becomes an authority

explanation: Synchronous search updates improve freshness while extending write latency; asynchronous indexing isolates writes but creates lag. The obligation travels with the choice, because derived stores may lag and interfaces must tolerate or disclose that lag. Freshness is what the synchronous option buys, and nothing about the indexing schedule moves the authority: search still consumes committed changes and stays rebuildable.

front: A cache, and a search system
back: A cache stores reusable results closer to demand; a search system builds specialized indexes for discovery and ranking. Both are derived-data systems.
What a derived-data system's value depends on — the same three for a cache and for a search index.

front: Where caches live, what search indexes consume
back: Caches may exist in browsers, CDNs, applications, and data services. Search indexes typically consume committed changes and serve query-oriented representations.

front: The steps a search system performs
back: It tokenizes, normalizes, indexes fields, filters, scores, and returns identifiers or projections.
A stampede sends many misses to the authority; a hot key overloads one shard.

prompt: A backup job has reported success on every run since it was set up, and nobody has ever restored from it. What does that record establish?

options.text: Only that the jobs ran and reported success — a restore drill is what verifies credentials, tooling, integrity, and elapsed time
That the backups are complete
options.feedback: Untested backups may be incomplete. A job reporting success is a statement about the job, not about what it produced.

options.text: That the keys needed to read the backups are available
options.feedback: Untested backups may be encrypted with unavailable keys. Nothing in a successful backup run exercises the keys on the way back.

options.text: That a restore would finish inside the recovery objective
options.feedback: Untested backups may be too slow to meet recovery objectives. Elapsed time is one of the things a restore drill measures, and a backup job never measures it.

explanation: Restore drills verify credentials, tooling, integrity, and elapsed time — not merely that backup jobs report success. Untested backups may be incomplete, encrypted with unavailable keys, or too slow to meet recovery objectives, and a long run of successful jobs tells none of those cases apart from a working one. Recovery is defined by explicit time and data-loss objectives, and only a drill measures against them.

prompt: Put the steps of this lesson's `full_name` replacement in order.

steps.text: Deploy code that writes both formats and reads new with old fallback

explanation: This is expand–migrate–contract at full length: add a backward-compatible shape, move readers and writers and backfill the data, then remove the old shape after no active version depends on it. Only the first and last steps touch the schema. The fallback in step two is what lets old and new code run side by side, and the ordering of the last three follows the rule the pattern states — the old shape goes only once nothing running still depends on it.

prompt: A `full_name` column has to be split and the service cannot be taken offline. Proposal A is expand–migrate–contract across several releases. Proposal B is one in-place destructive change, accepting a short outage to do it. Which of these are reasons to adopt A here?

options.text: Backward compatibility supports safe rolling deploys, which is what a service that cannot go offline needs
In-place destructive changes are simple only when downtime is acceptable, and here it is not
Durable systems must change without assuming all code and data update atomically, which is what this lesson takes B to assume
A avoids the temporary complexity that B would introduce
A removes the need to practice restoring a pre-migration backup

explanation: Backward compatibility increases temporary complexity but supports safe rolling deploys, and in-place destructive changes are simple only when downtime is acceptable — which settles the choice here, because it is not. Underneath both sits the reason the practice exists: durable systems must change without assuming all code and data update atomically. This lesson reads B as making that assumption, since an in-place change needs every reader and writer to move at once, and the outage is what would have enforced it. The rejected options invert the trade. A costs temporary complexity rather than avoiding it, and the instruction to practice restoring a pre-migration backup separately stands whichever proposal wins.

back: Migrations evolve live data and schemas. Backups preserve recoverable copies. Recovery turns those copies and logs into a working service within explicit time and data-loss objectives.
First add a backward-compatible shape, then move readers and writers and backfill data, then remove the old shape after no active version depends on it.
It avoids long exclusive locks and bounds backfills.
Replicas improve availability but can replicate corruption; independent backups preserve earlier states.
It needs an authority and reconciliation.

prompt: The API from the opening scene goes into a full design review, and five changes are proposed. Which of them does this lesson support?

options.text: Distinguish success, client correction, conflict, rate limiting, dependency failure, and unknown server failure in the response itself
Establish credentials and idempotency on the requests that need them
Publish a machine-readable description, so the contract can support validation, documentation, and client generation
Keep the single status, and put a richer error string in every body
Derive the resource shapes from the existing database tables, so the contract matches storage

explanation: Responses distinguish success, client correction, conflict, rate limiting, dependency failure, and unknown server failure. Requests identify an operation, carry typed input, and establish credentials and idempotency where needed. Machine-readable descriptions can support validation, documentation, and client generation. The two rejected proposals are the ones this lesson argues against directly: returning `200` for every outcome weakens generic tooling, and a richer body leaves that in place because anything reading the status never sees it. And design runs from use cases outward, never beginning with database tables.

prompt: A client team's code branches on a string inside the response body at every call site, because the status is identical whether a request succeeded, was malformed, or hit a conflict. Which failure does this lesson name?

options.text: Returning `200` for every outcome weakens generic tooling
Leaking internal exception text exposes implementation
options.feedback: That failure gives a caller too much of the wrong detail. Here the caller is given too little of the right detail, and nothing internal is exposed at all.

options.text: Changing enum meaning without versioning breaks clients even if the wire type is still a string
options.feedback: That failure is about a field whose meaning moved between releases. Nothing here changed; the outcomes were never distinguishable in the first place.

options.text: Unbounded filters or expansions create denial-of-service paths
options.feedback: A real failure of this API's operational limits, but it costs availability rather than legibility. The symptom described is a caller unable to tell outcomes apart.

explanation: Returning `200` for every outcome weakens generic tooling. Responses are supposed to distinguish success, client correction, conflict, rate limiting, dependency failure, and unknown server failure, and an API that collapses all six into one status leaves the distinction readable only by something that parses the prose.

prompt: Match each design choice to the cost this lesson attaches to it.

pairs.right: more data and behavior coupled together
more supported surfaces to keep alive

distractors: page boundaries that shift under concurrent inserts
implementation details visible in an error body
explanation: Coarse operations reduce round trips but couple more data and behavior. Fine-grained resources improve composition but create chatty workflows. Explicit versions simplify breaking change boundaries while multiplying supported surfaces. Tolerant reading helps evolution but can conceal misspelled fields. The two distractors are failure modes rather than the price of a deliberate choice: offset pagination becomes unstable under concurrent inserts, and leaking internal exception text exposes implementation.

back: A contract for requesting behavior or information across a boundary. Contracts let clients and providers change independently, and turn undocumented assumptions into reviewable decisions that can be tested and observed.

front: What good API design makes predictable
back: Vocabulary, identity, validation, errors, evolution, and operational limits.
Success, client correction, conflict, rate limiting, dependency failure, and unknown server failure.
Caller intent, then the authorized operation, then stable domain vocabulary, then transport representation — and not database tables or framework controller shapes.

front: An idempotency key on a create command
back: Repeated delivery of the same key returns the original result.

prompt: Match each name to what this lesson says it is.

pairs.right: an interface centered on resources and representations
an interface centered on a typed graph and a selection set
an interface centered on procedures and messages
a text interchange format, and not an interface style

distractors: a transport that removes distributed-system failure
a schema whose resolvers are generated from procedures
explanation: REST, GraphQL, and RPC are interface styles with different centers of gravity: standardized resource transfer, client-selected graph queries, and explicit remote operations. JSON is a language-independent text interchange format, not an API style, which is why comparing styles by contracts and workloads beats treating them as competing serialization formats. Neither distractor is on offer: none of the three styles removes distributed-system failure, and resolvers belong to GraphQL while generated clients belong to RPC.

prompt: A team runs the three boundaries from this lesson's example in three styles, and proposes one shared client configuration covering all of them. Which of these does the example say each boundary has separately?

options.text: Timeouts
Identity
Compatibility
Telemetry
Query-cost controls
A serialization format

explanation: The example closes on the sentence teams skip: each boundary has separate timeouts, identity, compatibility, and telemetry. Query-cost controls are something GraphQL specifically requires, alongside resolver batching and field-level policy, rather than something every boundary carries. And a serialization format is not what separates these boundaries at all — JSON is a language-independent text interchange format, not an API style.

prompt: A team moves an internal boundary to typed RPC with generated clients, and argues that the generated types now rule out compatibility breaks. Which sentence from this lesson corrects them?

options.text: Generated types can create false confidence when semantic compatibility still changes
RPC offers strong operation names and efficient schemas
options.feedback: True, and probably why the team chose RPC. It says nothing about what generated types do or do not guarantee.

options.text: RPC clients retry non-idempotent procedures automatically
options.feedback: A real RPC failure mode, but about what a client does after a call fails rather than about whether a contract has quietly changed meaning.

options.text: GraphQL requires query-cost controls, resolver batching, and field-level policy
options.feedback: Requirements belonging to a different style, and to a different problem than compatibility.

explanation: Generated types can create false confidence when semantic compatibility still changes: the types keep agreeing while the meaning underneath moves. It sits under the claim this lesson opens with — REST, GraphQL, and RPC are interface styles with different centers of gravity, and none of them removes distributed-system failure.

back: Interface styles with different centers of gravity: standardized resource transfer, client-selected graph queries, and explicit remote operations. None removes distributed-system failure.
Procedures and typed request and response messages, often with generated clients.

front: What GraphQL asks for in exchange
back: It reduces client over-fetching and under-fetching, but requires query-cost controls, resolver batching, and field-level policy.
Client composition, caching, observability, authorization, schema evolution, and how transport semantics map to application behavior.

front: Where REST-oriented HTTP gains, and where it costs
back: It gains from standard HTTP behavior, and can require multiple resources for one screen.

prompt: Two designs for a build system are on the table. Proposal A publishes the status event and then commits the status. Proposal B commits the status and then publishes an outbox event. Which does this lesson support, and on what grounds?

options.text: Proposal B, because publishing before a database commit exposes facts that may roll back
Proposal A, because publishing first shortens the delay before consumers see the change
options.feedback: Persistent connections are how this lesson buys update delay down. Publishing ahead of the commit buys it by announcing something that may turn out never to have happened.

options.text: Proposal B, because at-least-once delivery requires idempotent consumers
options.feedback: At-least-once delivery does require idempotent consumers, and both proposals need that equally. It is not what separates them.

options.text: Either, provided consumers deduplicate by event ID
options.feedback: Deduplication handles the same message arriving twice. A message describing a change that was later rolled back is not a duplicate, and deduplicating it changes nothing.

explanation: Publishing before a database commit exposes facts that may roll back, which is why the worked example commits build status and then publishes an outbox event. It follows from separating transport delivery from application truth: a message says “something was delivered”, an authoritative record says “this effect is committed”, and Proposal A lets the first sentence run ahead of the second.

prompt: Put the build system's steps into the order this lesson gives them.

steps.text: The build system commits the build status
Workers and notification consumers deduplicate by event ID
A browser client receives a hint over the stream, or misses it
After reconnect, the client refetches the current build representation

explanation: The commit comes first, because publishing before a database commit exposes facts that may roll back. Then the outbox event, then consumers that deduplicate by event ID rather than trusting the transport to deliver once. The browser sits on its own path at the end: a hint may simply not arrive, and the refetch after reconnect is what keeps a missed hint from corrupting state.

prompt: A team moves a queue from at-most-once delivery to at-least-once. According to this lesson, which of these now follow?

options.text: Consumers have to be idempotent
Consumers processing duplicates becomes a live concern
The possibility that work is simply lost goes away
Globally exactly-once business effects become available without further work
Ordering becomes global across partitions
Poison messages stop retrying forever

explanation: At-most-once delivery may lose work, and at-least-once requires idempotent consumers, so the move trades a loss risk for a duplication risk — both halves of that trade change on the day the switch is made. Consumers processing duplicates is one of this lesson's named failure modes, and the worked example answers it by deduplicating on event ID. The move does not reach the stronger promise: globally exactly-once business effects usually require narrower transactional definitions. The last two options are separate entries on the same failure list, unmoved by the delivery semantics — consumers assume global order across partitions, and poison messages retry forever.

back: Realtime delivers updates while a client remains interested; event-driven publishes facts or commands for asynchronous processing.

front: A message, against an authoritative record
back: A message says something was delivered; an authoritative record says this effect is committed.

front: What a consumer should be able to do
back: Reconnect, deduplicate, and reconstruct state.
Queues distribute jobs; append-only logs retain ordered records for consumer positions.
At-most-once may lose work; at-least-once requires idempotent consumers; globally exactly-once business effects usually require narrower transactional definitions.

prompt: Match each thing you might find at a boundary to what this lesson says was left undone.

pairs.left: A receiver that accepts any token whose signature verifies
A queued job still holding the credential it started with
A service that believes an identity header supplied by whoever called it
pairs.right: establish trust in the credential itself

pairs.left: An audit record naming only a shared account
pairs.right: carry the actor separately, in trace and audit context

distractors: authenticate the service instance with mutual TLS or platform workload identity
associate the browser with server state using a session credential
explanation: Three of these are a receiver obligation left undone. Each receiver must establish trust in the credential, constrain its audience and lifetime, and make its own authorization decision. A signature that verifies says nothing about the issuer and audience a signed access token can carry, so the audience was never constrained; a credential still sitting in a queued job is one whose lifetime was never bounded; and an identity header supplied by the caller is trust that was never established. The fourth is not an obligation but a missing mechanism — an audit naming only a shared account needs trace and audit context, which carries actor and delegation metadata separately from security credentials. Neither distractor helps: mutual TLS or platform workload identity authenticates service instances rather than narrowing what a credential opens, and session credentials associate a browser with server state.

prompt: In the worked example, the document service records both the reporting workload and the delegated user before applying its own resource permission. What does recording both accomplish that recording either one alone would not?

options.text: It names the caller and keeps the original actor, which no single record does
It lets the document service skip its own authorization decision, since the reporting API already made one
options.feedback: Each receiver must establish trust in the credential, constrain its audience and lifetime, and make its own authorization decision. Nothing upstream discharges that, which is why the example ends with the document service applying its own resource permission.

options.text: It extends the five-minute token's lifetime for as long as the report is being produced
options.feedback: Lifetime is a property of the exchanged token. What goes into an audit record does not reach back and change it.

options.text: It establishes that the reporting workload and the user are the same subject
options.feedback: They are deliberately not. A service may authenticate another service while acting on behalf of a user with narrower delegated permission — two subjects, one request.

explanation: Human identity, workload identity, and delegated authority are related but not interchangeable, so a record naming one of them is not a record of the others. Service credentials clearly identify the caller but can erase user context, and explicit identity design is what prevents audit records that lose the original actor. Recording both keeps “which workload called” and “on whose behalf” from having to be one answer.

prompt: A downstream document service must end up holding a credential it cannot present anywhere else, and cannot present for long. According to this lesson, which of these move toward that?

options.text: Exchange the incoming credential for one intended for that downstream audience
Give the issued token an audience naming only that service
Give the issued token a short lifetime
Forward the original user token unchanged
Authenticate the calling service instance with mutual TLS
Have the document service make its own authorization decision

explanation: Token exchange can replace a broad credential with one intended for a downstream audience, and short-lived, audience-specific tokens limit replay at the cost of issuance infrastructure. The worked example does all three at once: a session becomes a five-minute token valid only for the document service. Forwarding moves the other way, because propagating the original user token is simple but broadens its exposure and audience. Mutual TLS or platform workload identity authenticates service instances, which establishes who is calling rather than narrowing what the credential opens. And each receiver must make its own authorization decision in any case — that is required whatever credential arrives, so it constrains nothing about the credential.

back: Communicating who or what initiated work across a boundary.
The end actor, the calling workload, and the authority being exercised.

front: What every receiver owes at a boundary
back: Establish trust in the credential, constrain its audience and lifetime, and make its own authorization decision.
Replacing a broad credential with one intended for a downstream audience.

front: Forwarding the user token, or using service credentials?
back: Forwarding is simple but broadens the token's exposure and audience; service credentials clearly identify the caller but can erase user context.

prompt: An outbound call to a payment provider passes its deadline with no response. Before anything else happens, what has that established?

options.text: Nothing about whether the effect happened, because timeouts leave unknown outcomes
That the provider is unavailable, since a healthy provider answers inside the deadline
options.feedback: The deadline belongs to the outbound call, not to the provider. A timeout does not distinguish a request that never arrived from a response that never came back.

options.text: That the call did not reach the provider, so it is safe to send again
options.feedback: That is the assumption this lesson exists to remove. Sending again on that assumption is how provider retries duplicate work.

options.text: That the provider's rate limits were exceeded
options.feedback: API quotas cause cascading retries, which is a different failure with a different signature. A deadline passing says nothing about which limit, if any, was involved.

explanation: Timeouts leave unknown outcomes. That is the entire finding, and it is why the mental model asks you to persist enough local state to reconcile after timeouts or delayed callbacks: the unknown is not preventable, so the design has to survive it. A third-party integration places part of a workflow behind an independently operated contract, and the provider's availability and limits are not readable from this side of it.

prompt: A webhook handler verifies the signature, then does all of its work before responding, and never checks whether it has seen the event before. Which of the duties this lesson gives a webhook handler is it failing to perform?

options.text: Acknowledge quickly
Deduplicate event IDs
Process asynchronously
Verify origin or signatures
Map provider results into application outcomes

explanation: Webhooks verify origin or signatures, acknowledge quickly, deduplicate event IDs, and process asynchronously. This handler performs the first and none of the other three: work finished before the response is neither a quick acknowledgement nor asynchronous processing, and nothing looks at the event ID. Structured error mapping is a duty of outbound calls rather than of inbound webhooks — it is how provider results become application outcomes on the way back.

prompt: The payment adapter creates a local payment attempt and sends that attempt's ID to the provider. What does it send the ID as?
hints: The point is that sending it twice must mean the same attempt, not a second one.
It is one of the five things this lesson says outbound calls use.
explanation: A payment adapter creates a local payment attempt and sends its ID as the provider idempotency key. That is what makes a retry after the ambiguous timeout a question about the same attempt rather than a second one, which is the answer to provider retries duplicating work.

back: Part of an application workflow placed behind an independently operated contract.

front: What a provider brings with it
back: Its own availability, limits, security posture, release schedule, and data lifecycle.
It translates stable application intent into provider calls, and provider results into application outcomes.
Verifies origin or signatures, acknowledges quickly, deduplicates event IDs, and processes asynchronously.
Synchronous calls give immediate feedback but couple user latency and availability to the provider; asynchronous workflows remain responsive but expose pending states.

prompt: Put this lesson's threat-modeling mechanisms into the order it gives them.

steps.text: Draw the data flow: processes, stores, external actors, and boundaries
Write abuse cases describing attacker goals
Run the structured categories over what the diagram exposed
Give each control an owner and a way to verify it
Record the residual risk that is left

explanation: This is the order the lesson sets the mechanisms out in, taken from the order the source writes them; nothing here claims one of them is impossible without another. Data-flow diagrams expose processes, stores, external actors, and boundaries. Abuse cases describe attacker goals. Structured categories prompt review of impersonation, tampering, repudiation, disclosure, denial of service, and privilege escalation. Controls are assigned owners and verified through tests, monitoring, or operational drills. Residual risk is recorded rather than implied away.

prompt: The file-sharing model now lists guessed links, malicious file parsing, stale permissions, and resource exhaustion. Which of these does this lesson say still has to happen before those threats count as handled rather than listed?

options.text: Each control is assigned an owner
Each control is verified through tests, monitoring, or operational drills
Controls and telemetry attach to each path rather than to the product as a whole
Whatever risk is left over is recorded rather than implied away
The threat list is checked against a generic security checklist
The diagram is signed off so the model can be filed

explanation: Controls are assigned owners and verified through tests, monitoring, or operational drills, and residual risk is recorded rather than implied away. The file-sharing example supplies the fourth: controls and telemetry attach to each path, which is what makes visible a control that exists in documentation but not on every entry point. The two rejected proposals run against the lesson. The practice focuses security effort on how this system can fail rather than on a generic checklist alone, and a signed-off diagram put away is how the opening scene ended up with a model that had drifted.

prompt: A team's threat model considers only attackers arriving anonymously from the internet. Its diagram matches the current architecture, every control has an owner and a verification, and residual risk is written down. Which failure mode does this lesson name?

options.text: Teams model only anonymous internet attackers, ignoring insiders and compromised dependencies
Threats are listed without owners and verification
options.feedback: Every control here has an owner and a way to be checked. What is short is not the follow-through on a threat, but the range of actors considered at all.

options.text: Diagrams drift after architecture changes
options.feedback: The diagram matches. This model is current about a system it is only ever looking at from one direction.

options.text: A control exists in documentation but not on every entry point
options.feedback: That is a control that failed to reach everywhere it was needed. Here the controls are attached and verified; it is the list of who might act that stops early.

explanation: Teams model only anonymous internet attackers, ignore insiders and compromised dependencies, or list threats without owners and verification. This model does the second part well and the first part not at all. Threat models span browser, edge, backend, data, build, operations, people, and third parties — people and third parties included — and every data-flow boundary can change trust or privilege.

back: Identifying valuable assets, trust boundaries, plausible attackers, abuse paths, and controls before incidents reveal them — a repeatable design activity, not a one-time document.

front: The structured categories a threat review prompts
back: Impersonation, tampering, repudiation, disclosure, denial of service, and privilege escalation.
Probability, blast radius, detection time, or recovery time.

front: The three lenses on a threat model
back: Asset-centered analysis highlights impact, attacker-centered analysis highlights capabilities, and system decomposition finds boundary mistakes.
It should be proportional to risk, and usable enough that people do not bypass it.

prompt: An internal tool does not render a control for staff who lack the permission, and the API behind that control answers any request carrying a valid session. Which of this lesson's claims settles it?

options.text: Only server-side enforcement is authoritative
Multi-factor methods add independent evidence
options.feedback: Independent evidence strengthens confidence in who the caller is. Nobody here is unsure who called; what was never decided is whether that caller may do this.

options.text: Sessions bind authenticated state to a browser credential and support rotation and revocation
options.feedback: A session that rotates and revokes correctly still carries an identity rather than a permission. Revoking it would end the login, not supply the missing decision.

options.text: Passwords require salted, adaptive hashing and rate-limited verification
options.feedback: That protects the credential from being recovered or guessed. This request arrived with a perfectly good credential.

explanation: Authorization occurs throughout frontend affordances, APIs, domain operations, data access, jobs, and administration, and only server-side enforcement is authoritative. Checking permission only when rendering buttons is named here among the common causes of broken access control: an affordance is where authorization gets expressed to a person, not where it is enforced. A valid login never implies universal permission.

prompt: Match each choice this lesson offers to the cost it attaches to that choice.

pairs.right: consistent data, and decisions you can explain

distractors: permission that is only checked when a button is rendered
a credential holding more authority than it needs
explanation: Central identity providers reduce duplicated login logic but become critical dependencies. Role-based policy is understandable until role combinations explode. Attribute or relationship rules express context more precisely but require consistent data and explainability. Long sessions improve convenience, while short lifetimes and step-up checks reduce exposure. Neither distractor is the price of a deliberate choice: checking permission only when rendering buttons is a named cause of broken access control, and a credential with more authority than it needs is what deny by default exists to prevent.

prompt: Broken access control remains a leading web risk. Which of these does this lesson name among its common causes, rather than among the things that protect a credential?

options.text: Trusting object IDs
Checking permission only when rendering buttons
Stale authorization in long-lived tokens
Sessions that survive password reset unexpectedly
Verification that is not rate limited
Hashing that is neither salted nor adaptive

explanation: Common causes include trusting object IDs, checking permission only when rendering buttons, stale authorization in long-lived tokens, user enumeration, weak recovery flows, and sessions that survive password reset unexpectedly. The two rejected options belong to the other decision entirely: passwords require salted, adaptive hashing and rate-limited verification, which establishes confidence in an identity and settles nothing about what that identity may do. Keeping the two decisions separate is what prevents role checks from becoming identity checks.

back: Establishing confidence in an identity. It begins at login or workload credential issuance.
Deciding whether a principal may perform an action on a resource in the current context. A valid login never implies universal permission.
Roles, attributes, relationships, ownership, and explicit policy.
Give each credential only the authority it needs.
A second check that protects sensitive actions after risk changes.

prompt: Match each browser mechanism to what this lesson says it controls.

pairs.right: whether the application meant to send a request, rather than whether a cookie rode along
scope, cross-site sending, secure transport, and script access
verifying an external asset that does not change
whether a script may read selected responses from another origin
which sources a page may execute and load from

distractors: which destinations a page is permitted to navigate to
whether a direct HTTP client may call the API
explanation: CORS controls whether scripts can read selected cross-origin responses. Cookie attributes constrain script access, secure transport, cross-site sending, and scope. Content Security Policy restricts executable and loadable sources. Frame policy limits clickjacking. Subresource integrity can verify fixed external assets. CSRF defenses ensure a credentialed request reflects application intent, not merely that cookies were attached. Navigation is one of the policy areas the browser applies but not the job of any of these six, and the second distractor is the one that matters: browser-side checks are not protection against direct HTTP clients, so nothing in this column answers it.

prompt: A team moves its session out of a cookie and into a token its own JavaScript reads, and drops the CSRF policy because cookies are no longer attached automatically. What has this lesson's tradeoff already told them about the move?

options.text: Script injection now costs more, because the session is exposed to JavaScript
Nothing changes, because a bearer token and a cookie identify the same session
options.feedback: They identify the same session and they sit in different places. Cookie-based sessions integrate with browser protections; a token exposed to JavaScript does not, and that difference is the entire subject.

options.text: The application is now protected against clickjacking, because framing no longer carries the session
options.feedback: Frame policy is what limits clickjacking here, and it is a separate mechanism that this change does not touch.

options.text: Cross-origin scripts can now read the responses, because CORS no longer applies
options.feedback: CORS controls whether scripts can read selected cross-origin responses no matter where the session is kept. Moving the credential changes nothing about it.

explanation: Cookie-based sessions integrate with browser protections while requiring CSRF policy; bearer tokens exposed to JavaScript increase the consequences of script injection. These are not a safe option and a risky one but two different bills, and this team has traded a policy it had to build and keep for a standing exposure of the session to any script that runs on the page.

prompt: A second team copies the account app but serves the API from a separate origin behind a wildcard CORS header, and keeps the session in a token its scripts can read. Everything else in the design is unchanged. Which of the original's properties have they given up?

options.text: One origin for application and API, which simplifies credentials
A session credential the page's scripts cannot read
A cookie-based session that browser protections already apply to, along with the CSRF policy that goes with it
A restrictive Content Security Policy
Refusal to be framed
Sanitization of permitted rich text before insertion

explanation: The variant changed two things, and three properties go with them. Moving the API to a separate origin gives up the first: keeping application and API on one origin simplifies credentials, and multiple origins improve isolation when their content is genuinely untrusted, which an API you wrote is not. Moving the session into a readable token gives up the other two: HttpOnly is the attribute that constrains script access, one of the four things cookie attributes constrain, and cookie-based sessions integrate with browser protections while requiring CSRF policy, so the policy leaves with the cookie. The restrictive CSP, the refusal to be framed and the sanitization are untouched. And the wildcard is worth naming for what it is not — wildcard CORS mistaken for authentication is a failure mode here.

back: The scheme, host, and port tuple. Same-origin content has broad interaction; cross-origin interaction is constrained and selectively permitted.
An untrusted client, and at the same time a security enforcement environment.
Users, multiple origins, extensions, local state, and application servers.
It reduces injection impact but requires disciplined script delivery.

Through correct headers and content handling. The browser isolates web content primarily by origin while applying policies around scripts, network access, cookies, framing, navigation, and powerful capabilities.

prompt: Complete this lesson's path from input to output.
template: Parse shape, validate allowed meaning, preserve {{1}} data, then use a parameterized API or {{2}} for the exact output context.
hints: The third step is what keeps a value from being turned back into a string by accident.
The last step and the parameterized API are the two branches of an or, not a fallback for when the first is unavailable.
explanation: Parse shape, validate allowed meaning, preserve typed data, then use a parameterized API or encode for the exact output context. Preserving typed data is what keeps the first two steps from being undone: a value that stays an enum or a bounded date cannot be concatenated into somebody else's grammar by accident, because it is not a string yet.

prompt: In the report example, the title is inserted as text rather than HTML, and the export filename is generated from an internal ID rather than from the title. What do the two decisions have in common?

options.text: Each keeps a value from being read as syntax by the grammar it is entering
Each rejects the title as invalid input
options.feedback: Neither decision rejects anything. The title is accepted and displayed; the filter's own validation is the fixed enum and the bounded date range, which happen earlier and to different fields.

options.text: Each relies on a deny list of characters known to be dangerous
options.feedback: The model this lesson gives explicitly works without deny lists. Both decisions change how the value is constructed at its destination rather than which characters it may contain.

options.text: Each moves a check from the server to the client
options.feedback: Neither decision moves a check anywhere. Both change how a value is constructed at the boundary it is entering — the browser for the title, a filename grammar for the export.

explanation: Safety requires validation for meaning and context-appropriate construction or encoding at every interpreter boundary. Inserting the title as text is a DOM text API, which preserves text rather than parsing markup; generating the filename from an internal ID keeps a supplied string out of a filename grammar altogether. Both are safe construction rather than validation — validation asks whether data is allowed, and safe construction prevents it from becoming syntax.

prompt: A service validates every request body against a schema that bounds type, length, range, cardinality, and permitted values. Which of these does this lesson say the schema still does not do?

options.text: Stop a value it approved from becoming syntax once it is concatenated into another grammar
Encode a value for the exact output context it is eventually written into
Make a stored value safe in the admin interface that renders it later
Bound the permitted values a field may take
Reject a date range wider than the filter allows

explanation: Validation and encoding are complementary: validation asks whether data is allowed, and safe construction prevents it from becoming syntax. A schema that bounds type, length, range, cardinality, and permitted values has done the first job and none of the second. A safe value becomes unsafe after concatenation into another grammar, escaping for HTML text is reused in attributes or JavaScript, and stored payloads execute later in an admin interface — three failure modes that all begin with a value that passed validation. The two rejected options are exactly what schema validation does bound.

back: Data interpreted as commands or syntax by a downstream language.
HTTP parsers, application types, database queries, templates, browsers, file paths, command runners, and third-party APIs — each with its own grammar.
It separates SQL structure from values.
Required when a product intentionally accepts a constrained markup language, and rich text creates lasting security maintenance.
Sometimes necessary, but it should use argument arrays and fixed executables rather than shell strings.

prompt: A team can list every control they have switched on, and cannot say which credentials exist in production or who is able to change them. What does this lesson say they started without?
accept: an inventory of what enters production
hints: This lesson's model begins as one kind of list, and they built the other kind.
It is what the section heading puts before mechanism.
explanation: The model starts as an inventory rather than a control list, and its questions are what enters production, who can change it, how identity is established, where credentials exist, and how a compromised version is detected, revoked, and replaced. A list of switched-on controls can be complete and answer none of them.

prompt: A library the application depends on turns out to be vulnerable, and the team has to find it, rebuild, and roll out. Which of these does this lesson say makes that response possible?

options.text: Lockfiles and immutable artifact identifiers, which make dependency resolution reproducible
A software bill of materials describing the included components
Provenance connecting an artifact to the build process that produced it
Building once and promoting the same immutable artifact
A scanner report with no findings, which establishes that the dependency graph is safe
One credential shared across environments, so the rebuild can deploy anywhere

explanation: Lockfiles and immutable artifact identifiers make dependency resolution reproducible. Software bills of materials describe included components, and provenance can connect an artifact to its build process. The deployment example builds once and promotes the same immutable artifact, so the thing tested and the thing running are one object. Its payoff is exactly this response: a compromised library can be located, rebuilt, and rolled out without changing application configuration. The two rejected options are named failures rather than capabilities — automated scanning prioritizes known risk but does not prove safety, and one credential spanning environments is what turned the opening scene's deleted key into an incident.

prompt: A team wants to shorten the window in which a known-vulnerable dependency is still running, and they already have strong tests and a controlled rollout. Which of these choices does this lesson say shortens exposure?

options.text: Automatic updates
Vendoring every dependency
options.feedback: Vendoring improves availability and reviewability while increasing update work. It makes a dependency easier to read and its update slower to do, which is the wrong direction for exposure.

options.text: Pinning versions
options.feedback: Pinning versions improves reproducibility, and teams still need a process to advance pins. It fixes what is running rather than shortening how long a vulnerable version runs.

options.text: A managed build system
options.feedback: Managed build systems reduce maintenance but remain privileged dependencies. That is a choice about who operates the build, not about how fast a dependency can be moved.

explanation: Automatic updates shorten exposure but require strong tests and controlled rollout — the two things this team already has, which is what makes the choice available to them rather than merely attractive. Each of the four choices in that section buys something and leaves a job behind, and the job automatic updates leave is exactly those tests and that rollout control.

back: What connects source, build, artifact, deployment, and update systems. Compromise in any link can become application compromise.
Encrypts values, authenticates workloads, authorizes reads, rotates versions, and audits access.
Minimize trusted material, limit its authority and lifetime, verify provenance, and retain a practical response path when components are vulnerable.
Because consumers cannot overlap old and new credentials.
They reduce stored secrets; the deployment example authenticates to the cloud through short-lived workload identity.

prompt: A team needs evidence that one domain rule decides correctly. They write a browser journey that signs in, places an order, and cancels it, so that the rule runs at the end. Which of this lesson's claims says they reached too far?

options.text: Use the narrowest test that can disprove the important behavior
Add broader tests for boundary wiring and a small number of critical journeys
options.feedback: That is what breadth is for — wiring, and a few journeys. A single domain rule is neither, so this claim does not license the journey they wrote.

options.text: Production monitoring covers conditions pre-release tests cannot reproduce fully
options.feedback: That is about conditions no pre-release test can reproduce. A domain rule is deterministic behavior, which is exactly what a narrow test can disprove before release.

options.text: Tests should document expectations without freezing implementation details
options.feedback: A constraint on how a test is written rather than on how broad it should be. This journey freezes nothing internal; it is simply not the narrowest thing that could have disproved the rule.

explanation: Use the narrowest test that can disprove the important behavior, then add broader tests for boundary wiring and a small number of critical journeys. Unit tests exercise deterministic behavior through a module's public interface, which is what a single domain rule is. End-to-end tests observe a user journey through deployed components, and this rule is not a user journey.

prompt: Match each line of the order-cancellation example to what this lesson says that line is.

pairs.left: Focused tests on the cancellation rule
pairs.right: unit tests, through the module's public interface

pairs.left: A database test that verifies concurrency
pairs.right: an integration test, using a real boundary implementation

pairs.left: A check on the API's conflict semantics
pairs.right: a contract test, over assumptions shared by independently changing parties

pairs.left: A browser run that cancels and sees an accessible result
pairs.right: an end-to-end test, observing a user journey through deployed components

pairs.left: Cancellation errors tracked by reason after release
pairs.right: production monitoring, which is not a pre-release test at all

distractors: property tests, exploring invariants across generated inputs
human checks, which a strategy also chooses where to place
explanation: Unit tests exercise deterministic behavior through a module's public interface. Integration tests use real boundary implementations such as a database or HTTP adapter. Contract tests verify assumptions shared by independently changing parties. End-to-end tests observe a user journey through deployed components, and accessibility conformance applies to complete processes and full pages. The fifth line is not a test: production monitoring covers conditions pre-release tests cannot reproduce fully. Neither distractor appears in the example. Property tests explore invariants across generated inputs, and nothing here generates inputs; a testing strategy also chooses where human checks provide useful evidence, and no line of this example is one.

prompt: This lesson keeps two lists apart: prices a team decides to pay for a kind of evidence, and failure modes. Which of these does it name as failure modes?

options.text: Tests assert private calls
Excessive mocking verifies an imagined collaboration
Only happy paths are tested
Flaky tests become ignored signals
Real dependencies cost setup and diagnosis
Browser tests are slower

explanation: The failure modes named here are tests that assert private calls, share mutable fixtures, depend on timing, or pass when the feature is broken; excessive mocking that verifies an imagined collaboration; only happy paths being tested; flaky tests becoming ignored signals; and coverage percentages treated as correctness. The two rejected options are prices rather than failures. Real dependencies improve fidelity but cost setup and diagnosis, and browser tests catch integration and accessibility failures while being slower — both are bought deliberately for the evidence they produce.

back: A choice about where automated and human checks provide useful evidence about behavior. It favors stable public boundaries and risk over maximizing test counts or one test shape.
Useful for deliberate serialized structures, not as a substitute for semantic assertions.
It applies to complete processes and full pages, which is the level an end-to-end journey works at.
Making change safer, localizing defects, and documenting expectations without freezing implementation details.
They improve intent if they do not hide required fields.

prompt: A provider is midway through replacing an old implementation with a new one. For a while both are live, and one consumer has to be correct against either. Which of this lesson's mechanisms is aimed at exactly that?

options.text: Compatibility matrices
Schema checks
options.feedback: A schema check compares one shape against one expectation. It catches structural incompatibility and says nothing about what is answering at the same time as what.

options.text: Provider tests
options.feedback: Provider tests execute examples against the real boundary — the boundary as it stands at that moment, which is one of the two. The window is about both at once.

options.text: End-to-end suites
options.feedback: An end-to-end run traverses whichever implementation it happened to reach and asserts a user-visible outcome. It can fail without telling you that the two being live together was the reason.

explanation: Compatibility matrices cover versions that coexist during rollout, which is exactly the window described. Schema checks catch structural incompatibility. Provider tests execute examples against the real boundary. Consumer-driven contracts publish expectations for provider verification. End-to-end suites create isolated data, act through public interfaces, and assert user-visible outcomes.

prompt: An integration depends on a third party whose test environment is rate limited, billed per call, and occasionally unavailable. What does this lesson say most cases do about it?

options.text: Use recorded or simulated boundaries, plus a small live probe
Call the real third party on every run, because fidelity outranks the other costs
options.feedback: Testing real third parties does improve fidelity. The rate, cost, and instability are exactly why this lesson does not make it the default.

options.text: Leave the boundary untested and let the deployed journeys cover it
options.feedback: End-to-end tests traverse several contracts at once, so a failure there says the path broke without saying which contract did.

options.text: Publish a consumer-driven contract and have the third party verify it
options.feedback: Consumer-driven contracts publish expectations for provider verification and require governance. That is an arrangement between parties who agree to it, and it answers nothing about rate, cost, and instability.

explanation: Testing real third parties improves fidelity while adding rate, cost, and instability, so most cases use recorded or simulated boundaries plus a small live probe. This lesson reads the probe as the part that keeps the recording honest, and the recorded boundary as the part that keeps the suite runnable.

prompt: An end-to-end suite seeds each case through an internal setup endpoint, runs in an environment shared with other suites, and asserts by reading a database row once the journey finishes. Which of this lesson's requirements for end-to-end suites does it break?

options.text: Create isolated data
Act through public interfaces
Assert user-visible outcomes
Traverse several contracts at once
Justify its expense for a critical flow

explanation: End-to-end suites create isolated data, act through public interfaces, and assert user-visible outcomes. This suite breaks all three: tests call internal setup endpoints unavailable to users, shared environments leak state between runs, and a database row is not a user-visible outcome. The two rejected options are not requirements this description breaks. End-to-end tests traverse several such contracts at once whatever else they do, and whether a flow justifies the expense is a decision about which flows to cover.

back: It states supported inputs and observable outputs.
The subset of a provider contract actually relied upon.
They publish expectations for provider verification, revealing actual dependencies while requiring governance.
They execute examples against the real boundary.
Whether a real user goal survives the integrated path.

prompt: A team can already see that an error rate rose, and can read the individual failures one by one. What they cannot say is where inside a single failing operation the time went, or which call failed. Which of this lesson's signals are they missing?
hints: They already hold two of the four. Work out which question is the one left over.
The missing signal is the only one of the four whose question is about a single operation rather than about a count, an event, or code.
explanation: Metrics answer “how much or how often?”, which is what the error rate already gives them. Logs answer “what event occurred?”, which is what reading the individual failures gives them. Traces answer “where did this operation spend time and fail?”, and trace spans carry parent relationships, duration, status, and attributes — the only one of the four that follows a single operation. Profiles can answer “which code consumed resources,” which is a question about code rather than about this operation's path.

prompt: A team adds the user ID to their telemetry so a symptom can be connected to affected users. They put it on the log lines, on the trace spans, and on the metric as a dimension. Which of the three does this lesson say is the expensive one, and why?

options.text: The metric dimension, because cardinality drives metric memory cost
The trace spans, because a span already carries duration, status, and attributes
options.feedback: High-cardinality identifiers are useful in traces. An identifier arriving as one more span attribute is what traces are for.

options.text: The log lines, because free-form logs cannot be queried reliably
options.feedback: That is a different problem — an unstructured log line instead of typed fields. High-cardinality identifiers are useful in logs, and a typed field holding one is a structured log doing its job.

options.text: All three equally, since it is the same value in each place
options.feedback: It is the same value carrying different prices. High-cardinality identifiers are useful in traces and logs but expensive as metric dimensions.

explanation: High-cardinality identifiers are useful in traces and logs but expensive as metric dimensions; OpenTelemetry notes that cardinality drives metric memory cost. User IDs or raw paths explode metric cardinality, which is the named failure. On a log line or a span, the same identifier is what connects a symptom to affected users and dependencies.

prompt: Name the three shapes this lesson gives for aggregating measurements.
hints: Both missing words are metric shapes, not a log, a span, or an identifier.
The lesson names all three in a single sentence, and counters is the first of them.
explanation: Counters, gauges, and histograms aggregate measurements, which is how metrics answer “how much or how often?” The other entries in that same list are not metric shapes: structured logs use stable event names and typed fields, trace spans carry parent relationships, correlation identifiers link signals, sampling bounds cost, and semantic conventions make common operations comparable.

back: They use stable event names and typed fields.
